---
title: "Forms and validation"
---

Everything you have built so far reacts to a click. Real pages ask for
something first: a name, a number, a color. HTML has a wrapper for exactly
that, and the wrapper comes with a surprise built in. Meet it first.

## The page that throws your input away {#sec-forms-reload}

1. Create a new app from our template and call the folder `form-experiment`.
2. In `index.html`, replace everything between `<body>` and `</body>` with
   this:

   ```html
   <h1>Sign up</h1>
   <form id="signupForm">
     <label for="visitorName">Your name</label>
     <input id="visitorName" name="visitorName" type="text">
     <button id="sendButton" type="submit">Send</button>
   </form>
   <script src="./src/index.ts" type="module"></script>
   ```

3. Delete both lines in `src/index.ts`. The heading they talked to is gone,
   so the file stays empty for a moment.
4. Type your name into the field in the browser and click **Send**.

The page blinks and comes back with the field empty. Your name is not lost, it
moved: look at the address bar, which now reads
`http://localhost:5173/?visitorName=Lena`. Click into the field, type again,
and this time press Enter instead of clicking. Same blink, same address.

## Take the submit over {#sec-forms-preventdefault}

Now put this into `src/index.ts`:

```ts
const signupForm = document.querySelector<HTMLFormElement>('#signupForm');
const visitorName = document.querySelector<HTMLInputElement>('#visitorName');

if (!signupForm || !visitorName) {
  throw new Error('The sign-up page is missing an element');
}

signupForm.addEventListener('submit', (event) => {
  event.preventDefault();
  console.log(`Hello ${visitorName.value}`);
});
```

Open the browser console with F12, type a name, and press Enter. The page stays
where it is and your greeting shows up in the console. One line changed the
whole behavior.

## One event for the whole form {#sec-forms-submit}

A `<form>` is a box around the inputs that belong together. Its payoff is the
`submit` event: the browser fires it on the form when someone clicks a button
with `type="submit"` inside the form, and it fires the same event when someone
presses Enter in a text field. One listener on the form covers the mouse and
the keyboard, instead of a `click` listener on the button plus a `keydown`
listener on every input.

Every event comes with a default action, the thing the browser does on its own
unless your code objects. For `submit`, that default action is to send the
values to a web server and show the answer as a new page. Your form names no
server, so the browser sends the values back to the same page and loads it
again. That is the blink. The `name` attribute of each input is what turns
into `?visitorName=Lena` in the address.

`event.preventDefault()` cancels the default action. The event still happens
and your listener still runs, but the reload does not. From that line on, the
values are your code's business, and no input needs a `name` any more, because
you read `visitorName.value` yourself.

::: {.callout-warning}
## A page that blinks is a missing preventDefault

When your error message appears for a fraction of a second and then the page
looks new and empty, you forgot `event.preventDefault()`. Make it the first
line of every `submit` handler you write.
:::

## Labels are not decoration {#sec-forms-labels}

The line `<label for="visitorName">Your name</label>` points at the input whose
`id` is `visitorName`. Click the words in the browser and watch the cursor jump
into the field, because the label belongs to it now.

That connection is worth more than the bigger click target. A screen reader
announces "Your name" when the cursor enters the field, so a person who cannot
see the layout knows what to type. The browser tests you write in Part 8 look
inputs up by their label text, so a field without a label is a field the test
cannot find.

So: every input gets a `<label>`, and the label's `for` carries the input's
`id`.

## The rules an input can carry {#sec-forms-attributes}

An input can describe its own rules as attributes. `required` marks a field
that must not be empty. On `<input type="number">`, `min` and `max` describe
the range that makes sense. The browser reads those attributes and acts on
them, and the research box below sends you after the details.

Your code still has to check. No attribute knows that Lena is already on the
list, and none can compare one field with another. The form in the exercise
therefore carries `novalidate`, which tells the browser to stay out of the
checking and fire `submit` whatever the fields hold, so the only messages the
user reads are yours.

## Where the error goes {#sec-forms-errors}

An error nobody can see is not a message. Give the page one paragraph for it,
right below the form, and write into it with `textContent`. Add this line under
the `</form>` in `index.html`:

```html
<p id="signupError"></p>
```

Then look up that paragraph next to the other two elements and grow the
handler:

```ts
const signupError = document.querySelector<HTMLParagraphElement>('#signupError');

signupForm.addEventListener('submit', (event) => {
  event.preventDefault();

  const name = visitorName.value.trim();
  if (name === '') {
    signupError.textContent = 'Please enter your name.';
    visitorName.focus();
    return;
  }

  signupError.textContent = '';
  console.log(`Hello ${name}`);
  signupForm.reset();
});
```

Add `signupError` to the `if (!signupForm || !visitorName)` check as well, or
TypeScript reminds you that it can be `null`.

Read the shape of that handler, because every validating handler in this book
has it. Each rule gets its own `if`, which writes a message and then `return`s.
The good case lives at the bottom, where it can trust everything above it, and
its first move is to clear the message so yesterday's complaint does not sit
next to today's success.

Two small methods do the rest. `visitorName.focus()` puts the cursor back into
the field with the problem. `signupForm.reset()` puts every field back to the
value written in the HTML, which for an empty field means empty again.

## Two events while typing {#sec-forms-input-change}

The `submit` event is not the only way a form talks to you. The `input` event
fires on every single keystroke, so it is the one for feedback that should
follow along while the user types. The `change` event fires once the field is
finished, when the user leaves it or picks a value in a color or date picker.

`disabled` is an attribute in HTML and a property in TypeScript, and setting it
dims a button and stops it from firing clicks. Look the **Send** button up the
way you looked the other elements up, then keep it in step with the field:

```ts
visitorName.addEventListener('input', () => {
  sendButton.disabled = visitorName.value.trim() === '';
});
```

A disabled button is friendlier than an error message, because the user never
runs into the rule at all. It does not replace the check in the handler though.
Anyone can switch that attribute off in the browser's developer tools, so a
rule that lives only in the HTML is a rule you cannot count on.

::: {.research title="What can an input be?"}
The exercise below reads an age from a number field and refuses anything
outside 0 to 120. The chart you build in the next part goes further and asks
for a color, a position, and a size.

1. The `type` attribute of `<input>` has many possible values. Name three
   besides `text` and describe what the browser shows for each. Make sure
   `number`, `color`, and `range` are among the ones you can describe, because
   the next part's chart needs exactly those.
2. A number input has a `value` and a `valueAsNumber`. What does
   `valueAsNumber` give you that `value` does not, and what do you get from it
   while the field is empty?
3. What do `min`, `max`, and `step` do on `<input type="number">`? And can the
   field still end up holding a number outside `min` and `max`?

Questions 2 and 3 are exam material: you write validation code with no internet
and no AI next to you.
:::

## Exercise: the guest list {#sec-forms-exercise}

Build a form that collects guests for a party and rejects bad entries: no
empty names, no name twice, and no age of 700.

{{< exercise guest-list >}}

::: {.callout-tip}
## Helper functions and the null check

Write every helper of your own as `const showError = (message: string) => {
... };`. TypeScript keeps the null check from the top of the file alive inside
an arrow function stored in a `const`. Write the same helper as
`function showError(...) { ... }` and your elements are `possibly 'null'`
again, because such a function could also run before the check did.
:::

1. Open `index.html` and read it: a form with two labeled inputs, and below
   it an empty error paragraph, an empty `<ul>`, and an empty counter
   paragraph. Run `npm start` and click **Add guest**. The page reloads,
   exactly like the experiment at the start of this chapter.
2. In `src/index.ts`, import the stylesheet with `import './styles.css';`.
   Then look up the seven elements you need with `querySelector<...>`:
   `#guestForm`, `#guestName`, `#guestAge`, `#guestError`, `#guests`,
   `#guestCount`, and `#addGuest`. One `if` that throws covers all seven. The
   steps below call them `guestForm`, `nameInput`, `ageInput`, `errorText`,
   `guestList`, `countText`, and `addButton`.
3. Listen for `submit` on the form, call `event.preventDefault()` as the first
   line, and `console.log` the name for now. Expected result: clicking **Add
   guest** no longer reloads the page, and the name shows up in the console.
4. Refuse an empty name. Read `value`, cut the spaces off with `trim()`, and
   when nothing is left, write `Please enter a name.` into the error paragraph,
   focus the name field, and `return`.
5. Refuse a name that is already on the list, ignoring upper and lower case,
   so `lena` does not get in while `Lena` is there. Two ways work: keep an
   array of the names you added, or loop over the entries already in the list
   and compare their text. Pick whichever you find clearer.
6. Refuse an impossible age. Read the number with `valueAsNumber`, catch the
   empty field with `Number.isNaN`, and refuse anything below 0 or above 120.
   One message such as `Please enter an age between 0 and 120.` covers all
   three cases.
7. Now the good case. Clear the error paragraph, then build the entry: an `li`
   that holds a `span` with the class `guest-name` for the name, a second
   `span` with the age in parentheses, and a **Remove** button whose click
   listener removes the `li`. Append the `li` to `guestList`. Expected result:
   a line reading `Lena (17) Remove`, with the name in bold. If you chose to
   loop over the list in step 5, the class `guest-name` is what your loop looks
   for.
8. Keep the counter honest. Write a helper that puts the number of entries and
   the word `guests` into `countText`, such as `3 guests`, and call it when the
   page loads, after adding an entry, and after removing one. Expected result:
   the page says `0 guests` before you add anything.
9. Finish the good case with `reset()` on the form and `focus()` on the name
   field, so the next guest can be typed without touching the mouse.
10. Bonus: keep **Add guest** disabled while the name field is empty. Listen
    for `input` on the name field and set `addButton.disabled` from
    `nameInput.value.trim() === ''`. Do not forget the moment the page loads
    and the moment after a successful add.
11. Run `npm run check` and fix what Biome complains about.

The stylesheet keeps a line of height free for the error paragraph, so the
list does not jump while you test. Try every rule once: an empty name, a
duplicate, an empty age, an age of 700, and a good guest.

That form is the shape of the one waiting in the next part, where the fields
pick a color, a position, and a size, and what grows below them is a chart
instead of a list.
